title: URL Shortener
blurb: Read-heavy service: ID generation, caching, redirects, analytics

explanation.summary: Turns a long URL into a short code and redirects anyone who opens the code. It is a classic read-heavy system: one link is created once and opened many times, so the design is mostly about fast lookups.

title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
blurb: Authentication vs authorization, roles, permissions, JWT claims

explanation.summary: Instead of granting permissions to each user, you grant them to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and give users roles. Access checks become "does any of this user's roles include this permission?".

title: Uber Surge Pricing & Artificial Scarcity
blurb: Supply and demand per hexagon, gamed logouts, and how to price robustly

explanation.summary: Surge pricing raises the price where riders outnumber free drivers, to pull more drivers in. Because the price reacts to supply, drivers can fake a shortage by going offline together: artificial scarcity. A robust design prices from smoothed, sanity-checked supply and locks the price the rider sees.

title: Docker vs Virtual Machines
blurb: Hypervisors vs shared kernels, images, layers, and when to use which

explanation.summary: A virtual machine emulates a whole computer and boots its own operating system. A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel. VMs give stronger isolation; containers are far lighter and start in about a second.

title: Twitter Timeline & Search
blurb: Fan-out on write, celebrity merge at read time, caching and search
chapters: Step 4: Write API → Fan Out Service
Step 6: Fan Out Service → Search Cluster
Step 7: Fan Out Service → Notification Service

explanation.summary: Users post tweets, read a home timeline built from everyone they follow, and search. Reads dwarf writes, so the home timeline is precomputed: each new tweet is pushed into followers' timelines in memory (fan-out on write), except for celebrities, whose tweets are merged in when a timeline is read.

title: Web Crawler & Search
blurb: Priority frontier, duplicate detection, reverse index, freshness

explanation.summary: A crawler keeps a priority queue of links, fetches the most important page, skips it if a near-identical page was already crawled, and otherwise queues it for indexing. Search reads only the reverse index (word → pages) and the stored titles and snippets.

title: Kafka: Event Streaming
blurb: Topics, partitions, consumer groups, replication and delivery guarantees

explanation.summary: Kafka is a distributed, durable log. Producers append events to topics, which are split into partitions spread across brokers; consumers read them at their own pace and remember where they are with offsets. It decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes, and lets many systems react to the same events.

title: Idempotent Payments
blurb: "Payment failed" but money debited: lost responses, retries and idempotency keys

explanation.summary: A payment can succeed at the bank while its response is lost on the way back, so the app cannot tell success from failure. If it retries as a new request, the customer pays twice. The fix: the app sends an idempotency key, the server remembers the first result for that key and replays it, and a timeout is treated as "pending" and settled later by webhooks and reconciliation.

title: Mint: Personal Finance Aggregator
blurb: Pulling bank transactions through a queue, then categorizing and budgeting them

explanation.summary: Mint connects to a user's bank accounts, pulls their transactions, sorts each one into a category, and warns them when a monthly budget is close to its limit. The hard part is the pipeline: many slow, unreliable bank connections feeding a steady flow of writes. An extraction service, a queue, and small services for categories and budgets keep the user-facing side fast.

title: Pastebin
blurb: Short keys, metadata in SQL, text in an object store, expiry and caching

explanation.summary: A user pastes text and gets a short link; anyone with the link can read it until it expires. The text sits in an object store, a small row in SQL records the key and expiry, a cache serves hot pastes, and a background job removes expired ones.

title: Key-Value Store (Dynamo-style)
blurb: Hash ring, replication, quorum reads and writes, hinted handoff and LSM storage

explanation.summary: A key-value store only offers get(key) and put(key, value), which lets it spread over many machines and keep working when some fail. Keys are placed on a hash ring, each key is copied to N nodes, and quorum rules (W acks to write, R replies to read) let you choose between speed and fresh reads.

title: Social Network Graph
blurb: Friend lists across Person Servers, a lookup service, and shortest-path search

explanation.summary: A social network is a graph of people and friendships. The key feature is finding the shortest path between two people. The friend lists are too big for one machine, so they are split across Person Servers, a Lookup Service says which server holds whom, and a breadth-first search walks the graph in batches.

title: Amazon's Sales Rank by Category
blurb: Batch MapReduce over transaction logs, a ranked table, and a cache in front

explanation.summary: Each category shows its bestsellers for the past week. Purchases are appended to log files, a batch MapReduce job adds them up per category and product on a schedule, and the sorted result is stored in an analytics table and cached. Shoppers read the finished table, so reading is fast and the order path is untouched.

title: Query Cache for a Search Engine
blurb: LRU caching, sharded memory, TTLs and invalidation for hot searches

explanation.summary: A search engine answers the same popular queries again and again. Computing each answer means reading posting lists and fetching documents, which is slow. So the Query API keeps the results of recent queries in a sharded in-memory cache with LRU eviction, and only searches the index on a miss.

title: Scaling to Millions of Users on AWS
blurb: From one server to a load-balanced, cached, sharded fleet, one bottleneck at a time

explanation.summary: No system starts at millions of users. This topic follows one app from a single server to a sharded fleet, adding one idea at each stage: split the database off, balance and cache, auto scale and go async, then shard. You add each piece only when a measured number runs out.

title: Rate Limiter
blurb: Token bucket, fixed and sliding windows, and what to do when the counter store is down

explanation.summary: A rate limiter caps how many requests a caller can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and overload, keeps one noisy client from starving the rest, and enforces paid plans. The hard parts are choosing the counting algorithm, counting correctly across many servers, and deciding what happens when the counter store is down.

title: Consistent Hashing
blurb: How a cache or database cluster adds and loses nodes without reshuffling every key

explanation.summary: Consistent hashing is a way to spread keys over a changing set of servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys. Servers and keys are hashed onto the same ring; a key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. It is used by caches, sharded databases, CDNs and load balancers.

title: Chat System (WhatsApp-style)
blurb: WebSockets, store-then-deliver, groups, presence and offline push

explanation.summary: Users keep a WebSocket open to a gateway. A sent message is stored first, then delivered through a queue to the gateway holding the recipient's connection. Offline users get a push notification and catch up from their last message id when they return.

title: CDN: Content Delivery Network
blurb: Edge caches, cache keys and TTLs, shielding the origin, purging and hit ratio

explanation.summary: A CDN is a worldwide network of caches placed close to visitors. The first request for a file travels to your origin; the copy is kept at the edge, so later requests are answered a few kilometres away. It cuts latency, shields the origin from load and absorbs traffic spikes and attacks.

title: Notification System
blurb: Push, email and SMS at scale: dedup, preferences, queues, retries and dead letters

explanation.summary: A notification system turns events ("your order shipped") into messages on the right channel (push, email, SMS) without annoying people or losing important ones. The core design is: accept events fast, check preferences, put messages on per-channel queues, and let workers deliver them with retries.

title: Unique ID Generator (Snowflake)
blurb: Time-sorted 64-bit ids from many machines, with no coordination and no duplicates

explanation.summary: Every row needs an id that nobody else will ever use, even when many servers create rows at the same time. A Snowflake-style generator packs the time, the machine and a counter into one 64-bit number, so each machine can make ids alone, with no database and no talking to the others.

title: Search Autocomplete (Typeahead)
blurb: Prefix trie with precomputed top-k, layered caches, and a pipeline that learns from searches

explanation.summary: Autocomplete shows likely searches as the user types. Each keystroke is a prefix lookup that must come back in roughly 100 ms, for billions of searches. The design has two halves: a fast serving path (caches in front of an in-memory trie that already knows the top suggestions for every prefix) and a slow learning path that turns the query log into a fresh trie.

title: Proximity Service (Nearby Places)
blurb: Find places within a radius of you in milliseconds, using geohash cells instead of scanning every row

explanation.summary: Apps like Yelp and Google Maps must answer "what is near me?" in milliseconds out of hundreds of millions of places. The trick is to cut the map into labelled cells (geohashes) and keep a list of places per cell, so a search reads a few small lists instead of scanning every row.

title: Video Streaming (YouTube-style)
blurb: Chunked upload, transcoding into a bitrate ladder, adaptive streaming and CDN delivery

explanation.summary: A video platform has two jobs. The upload path accepts a huge file, converts it into many sizes and splits each into short segments. The playback path hands every viewer the right size, a few seconds at a time, from a cache close to them. Storage is cheap; delivering the bytes is the expensive part.

title: Metrics & Monitoring System
blurb: Collecting millions of samples a second, storing them as compressed time series, and alerting without false pages

explanation.summary: A monitoring system collects numbers from every server (CPU, requests, errors, latency), stores them as time series, draws them on dashboards and wakes someone when something is wrong. The write load is huge and steady, reads are mostly recent data, and the alerting path must keep working exactly when everything else is on fire.

title: File Sync (Dropbox-style)
blurb: Block-level sync: chunk and hash files, upload only what changed, and tell other devices

explanation.summary: A sync service keeps the same folder identical on all of a person's devices. The trick is to never treat a file as one lump: cut it into blocks, name each block by a hash of its bytes, and send only the blocks the server does not already have. A small metadata record says which blocks make up each version of each file.

title: Leader Election (Raft)
blurb: How a cluster agrees on one leader: terms, votes, heartbeats and fencing

explanation.summary: Many systems need exactly one node in charge: the primary of a database, the owner of a shard, the holder of a lock. Leader election lets a group of nodes agree on that one node, and agree again quickly when it fails. Raft does it with terms, votes from a majority, and heartbeats.

title: Locking: Redis & Database
blurb: Shared, exclusive, update and intent locks, Redis locks with fencing, and when to use which

explanation.summary: When two requests read the same thing and then change it, both can act on a value that is already out of date. A lock makes them take turns. Databases lock rows and tables for you; Redis can lock anything by name across many servers, but only for a limited time.

title: Distributed Cache
blurb: Cache-aside on a sharded Redis cluster: hash slots, eviction policies and cache stampedes

explanation.summary: A distributed cache keeps hot data in the memory of several servers, so most reads never touch the database. The hard parts are splitting keys across servers, choosing what to throw out when memory is full, keeping the cache from going stale, and not letting a burst of misses crush the database.

title: Database Sharding
blurb: How to split one table over many databases, and why the choice of shard key decides everything

explanation.summary: Sharding splits one large table into pieces (shards) and puts each piece on its own database server. A shard key decides which shard owns a row, and a router sends each query to the right shard. It lets storage and write traffic grow beyond one machine, at the price of harder queries, joins and transactions.

title: RAG Pipeline
blurb: Answering from your own documents: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking and citations

explanation.summary: A language model only knows its training data. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds the passages of your own documents that answer a question, puts them in the prompt, and asks the model to answer only from them, with citations.

title: Vector Database
blurb: Finding the nearest of 100 million embeddings in milliseconds: flat scans, HNSW, IVF-PQ, recall and filters

explanation.summary: An embedding model turns a photo or a sentence into a list of numbers that captures what it means. A vector database stores millions of these and finds the ones nearest to a query in milliseconds, by searching an approximate index instead of comparing with every vector.

title: LLM Gateway
blurb: One front door for every model: keys and budgets, routing, token limits, fallbacks, caching and guardrails

explanation.summary: An LLM gateway sits between a company's apps and the model providers they call. It holds the real API keys, gives each team its own virtual key and budget, routes each request to a suitable model, caches safe answers, keeps calls under the providers' token limits, fails over when a provider is down, masks personal data and logs the cost of every call.

title: AI Agent with Tools
blurb: A language model in a loop that calls tools: step limits, tool policy, prompt injection and idempotent actions

explanation.summary: An AI agent is a language model in a loop that can call tools: functions such as searching, booking or sending email. The model decides the next step; a runtime around it runs the tools, feeds the results back, and enforces what the model may do, how long it may run and which actions need a person.

title: AWS VPC Networking
blurb: Your own network in AWS: CIDR ranges, public and private subnets, route tables, NAT gateways and endpoints

explanation.summary: A VPC (virtual private cloud) is a private network in an AWS region with an address range you choose. You split it into subnets in several availability zones, and route tables decide where traffic from each subnet can go: to the internet, through a NAT gateway, to an AWS service endpoint, or only inside the VPC.

title: Application Load Balancer
blurb: One HTTPS entry point for many services: listeners, rules, target groups, health checks and routing algorithms

explanation.summary: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is AWS's HTTP load balancer. Listeners accept connections on a port and terminate TLS; rules match each request's host, path or headers and forward it to a target group; health checks keep broken targets out of rotation.

title: ECS on Fargate
blurb: Running containers without servers: task definitions, services, autoscaling on CPU and safe rolling deploys

explanation.summary: Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) runs containers as tasks, kept at a desired count by a service and registered with a load balancer. On Fargate, AWS supplies a small VM per task, so there are no servers to manage; you choose CPU and memory per task and pay for them by the second.

title: Full-stack App on ECS
blurb: A Vue client and Node API on ECS with DynamoDB and S3, shipped by CodePipeline with blue/green deploys

explanation.summary: A complete AWS setup for a web app: a Vue.js client and a Node.js API as two ECS services behind their own load balancers, DynamoDB and S3 for data, and a CodePipeline that builds every commit with CodeBuild and releases it with CodeDeploy blue/green deployments, all described in Terraform.

title: Load Balancer
blurb: Spreading requests over servers: algorithms, health checks and failover

explanation.summary: A load balancer sits in front of a group of identical servers and hands each request to one of them. It lets you add servers to handle more traffic, stops sending traffic to servers that have failed, and hides all of that behind a single address.

title: Redis Basics: Data Types
blurb: Strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets, with TTLs and atomic commands, by real use case

explanation.summary: Redis is an in-memory data store. Instead of plain values, it stores data types (strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets) with commands that change them in place, and it runs one command at a time, so each command is atomic. Keys can expire on their own.

title: Redis Persistence and Replication
blurb: RDB snapshots, the AOF, replicas, Sentinel failover and split brain: what each failure really loses

explanation.summary: Redis keeps data in memory, so what survives a failure depends on two separate choices: persistence (RDB snapshots and the append-only file) decides what a restarted node still has, and replication with Sentinel decides whether another node takes over, and how fast. Replication is asynchronous, so failovers and network splits can lose acknowledged writes.

title: AWS Basics: What the Cloud Is and Why
blurb: Buying servers vs renting them, regions and Availability Zones, Auto Scaling and Lambda, and what each costs

explanation.summary: AWS (Amazon Web Services) rents out computing, such as servers, storage, databases and networking, by the hour or by the request. Instead of buying hardware for your peak and waiting weeks for more, you start what you need in minutes, spread it across data centres, and pay for what you use. The trade-off is a bill that you have to design for and watch.

title: AWS IAM: Who Can Do What
blurb: Users, roles and JSON policies, and how AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, resource policies and permissions boundaries

explanation.summary: IAM (Identity and Access Management) decides whether each AWS API call is allowed. Every call is signed by an identity: a user, or a role with temporary credentials. AWS gathers the policies that apply (identity policies, resource policies, permissions boundaries and organisation SCPs) and evaluates them: an explicit Deny anywhere wins, and without an Allow the answer is no.

title: Disaster Recovery Across AWS Regions
blurb: RTO and RPO, the four AWS strategies from backup-and-restore to active/active, and why replicas are not backups

explanation.summary: Disaster recovery (DR) is how a system comes back after losing a whole region or its data. Two targets drive the design: RTO, how long it may be down, and RPO, how much recent data it may lose. AWS describes four strategies, from backup-and-restore (cheap, hours) to multi-site active/active (costly, near zero), and none of them replaces point-in-time backups.

title: Kafka Basics: Topics, Partitions, Groups
blurb: Events in an append-only log: keys pick partitions, consumer groups share them, offsets let anyone replay

explanation.summary: Kafka stores events in topics: append-only logs split into partitions. A key's hash picks the partition, which keeps each key's events in order. Consumers in a group share the partitions, one consumer per partition, and save their position as offsets, so many groups can read the same events, and any of them can rewind.

title: Kafka Reliability: Durability, Exactly-Once
blurb: ISR, acks and min.insync.replicas, unclean leader election, idempotent producers, transactions and rebalances

explanation.summary: Kafka's guarantees come from configuration. Replication with acks=all and min.insync.replicas decides which confirmed messages survive a broker failure; unclean leader election chooses between availability and data; idempotent producers remove duplicates from retries; and transactions make read-process-write exactly-once within Kafka.

title: Terraform Basics: Plan, Apply, State
blurb: Infrastructure as code: resources, the dependency graph, in-place vs replace, drift, and why the state file matters

explanation.summary: Terraform turns .tf files describing the infrastructure you want into API calls that make it so. It keeps a state file mapping each resource in the code to a real one, refreshes it, diffs the code against it, and shows a plan: create, update in place, replace or destroy. Apply follows the dependency graph and writes the new state.

title: Terraform Remote State and Locking
blurb: Why state lives in S3, how a lock stops two applies colliding, and what orphans and stale locks look like

explanation.summary: Terraform's state file is its memory of what it manages, so a team must share one copy and never write it twice at once. A remote backend such as S3 shares it, versioning keeps every revision, and a lock makes concurrent runs wait. When runs die, locks and orphaned resources need deliberate cleanup.

title: Terraform Modules and Environments
blurb: Copy-paste vs workspaces vs versioned modules: blast radius, promotion from dev to prod, and guarding against destroy

explanation.summary: Terraform modules package resources behind input variables and outputs, so one component can be reused across environments. How you lay out environments decides the blast radius of every change: copied folders drift, workspaces share one code version, and versioned modules with a root configuration and state per environment let changes be promoted and mistakes contained.
